paragraphs.heading: What an ester is
paragraphs.text: An ester comes from an acid, organic or inorganic, when the hydrogen of at least one acidic hydroxyl group, −OH, is replaced by an organyl group. For example, a carboxylic acid, R−C(=O)−OH, can react with an alcohol, R′−OH, in a substitution reaction that yields the ester R−C(=O)−O−R′. Formulas of such esters are usually written RCO₂R′ or RCOOR′, with R from the acid and R′ from the alcohol.

paragraphs.heading: How esters get their names
paragraphs.text: The German chemist Leopold Gmelin coined the word ester in 1848, probably by shortening the German Essigäther, meaning acetic ether. An ester's name is built from the alcohol and the acid it comes from. Esters of the simplest carboxylic acids usually keep trivial names such as formate, acetate, propionate and butyrate, rather than the IUPAC forms methanoate, ethanoate, propanoate and butanoate. Butyl acetate, for example, derived from butanol and acetic acid, is written CH₃CO₂(CH₂)₃CH₃.

paragraphs.heading: Shape and polarity
paragraphs.text: The carbonyl group, C=O, in these esters gives C–C–O and O–C–O angles of 120°. Rotation about the C–O–C bonds meets little resistance, so unlike amides, esters are flexible. That flexibility and low polarity mean they melt and boil at lower temperatures than the matching amides. In polarity, esters sit between ethers, which are less polar, and alcohols, which are more polar; and they can accept hydrogen bonds but cannot donate them.

paragraphs.heading: Pleasant smells
paragraphs.text: Esters of carboxylic acids usually smell pleasant, and those with low molecular weight are widely used as fragrances and turn up in essential oils and pheromones. Lactones are esters closed into a ring, and the ones found in nature mostly have 5- or 6-membered rings. Lactones help give fruits, butter, cheese and vegetables such as celery their aromas.

paragraphs.heading: Esters in living things
paragraphs.text: Esters matter in biology. Glycerides, the esters that fatty acids form with glycerol, are one of the main classes of lipids and make up the bulk of animal fats and vegetable oils. Esters of phosphoric acid form the backbone of DNA. ATP is an ester too, formed from triphosphoric acid.

paragraphs.heading: Solvents, plastics and explosives
paragraphs.text: Esters work as high-grade solvents for many plastics, plasticizers, resins and lacquers, and they are one of the largest groups of synthetic lubricants on sale. Polyesters are important plastics whose monomers are linked by ester groups. Some esters of nitric acid, such as nitroglycerin, are known as explosives.
